prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a leaking washing machine damaging the floor. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the washing machine has clearly been leaking over time rather than from a single sudden burst, I should treat the affected floor as a gradual escape of water issue and look for signs of repeated wetting, staining and swelling before I decide on cover."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the leak source is the appliance itself, I should check whether the damage extends beyond the machine footprint, because water often runs under nearby units and skirtings before the member notices it."},{"type":"observation","content":"When laminate or engineered wood flooring has cupped, lifted or gone soft after a leak, I should assume drying alone is unlikely to restore it and assess likely replacement rather than repair."},{"type":"preference","content":"When there is a mix of old wear and new water damage, I prefer to separate what was already deteriorated from what the leak actually caused so the claim outcome stays fair and within delegated authority."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the washing machine hose, inlet valve or waste connection is the apparent source, I should ask whether the installation was loose, perished or disturbed, because that often changes the pattern of damage and the documentation I need."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the floor is concrete with a floating finish, I should remember that visible surface staining may be limited even if the subfloor or underlay is badly affected, so I should not rely on appearance alone."},{"type":"preference","content":"When photos show the machine still in place, I prefer to ask for images after it has been moved if it can be done safely, because hidden moisture and damage behind or beneath it are easy to miss."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the leak has affected only the kitchen or utility room floor and not nearby walls or fittings, the likely scope is often narrower, so I should keep my assessment proportionate to the area actually exposed to water."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the member reports a damp smell or softening but no visible standing water, I should treat that as a prompt to consider underfloor saturation and possible delayed deterioration rather than dismissing the claim."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I am
